chapter.title: Asking the model to explain the change

cards.body:
To a diff, a 20% price rise and a fixed typo look the same: one line out, one line in. The scissors can cut, but they can't read.

So today the reader at the clipping service gets **only the clippings, plus a strict rule for the note**. That small pile is what makes the note good.
cards.simpler: A diff is a tool that spots which lines on a page changed. To a diff, a 20% price rise and a fixed typo look the same: one line out, one line in. It's like a pair of scissors that can cut but can't read. So today the reader at the clipping service gets **only the clippings, plus a strict rule for the note**. That small pile is what makes the note good.

cards.prompt: Overnight, your agent finds 2 changed lines on a rival's pricing page. Before we get to the rule, what should it hand to the model?

options.text: Both full versions of the page, about 4,000 words, to be safe
Just the 2 changed lines, plus a short instruction
The rival's entire website, so nothing gets missed

whyNot.a: That's the whole newspaper, not the clipping. The model has to hunt for the change and may describe parts that never moved.
whyNot.c: That's the whole newsstand, not the clipping. More text gives the model more places to wander off.

cards.reteach: The diff is the scissors, and it has already cut out what's new. Give the model just that clipping and it can't drift into the parts of the page that stayed the same. Less to read means less to guess.

cards.title: Less text, better answers
cards.body:
A *prompt* is the instruction you give the model, in plain English. For this job it has two parts: the changed lines from your diff, and a short rule for what to write back.

You'd think more context would help. Here it mostly hurts. Give the model a 3,000-word page and it has to guess which words matter. It may happily describe a feature that's been there for two years.

Give it **only the changed lines** and there's nothing to guess. It's a reader with one clipping on the desk instead of the whole Sunday paper.
cards.simpler: A prompt is the instruction you give the model in plain English. Here it has two parts: the changed lines, and a short rule for the reply. More text sounds helpful, but here it mostly hurts. Hand the model a 3,000-word page and it must guess what matters. It may describe a feature that's been there two years. Give it **only the changed lines** and there's nothing to guess. It's one clipping on the desk instead of the whole Sunday paper.

cards.title: Tidyhive's two edits
cards.body:
Take Tidyhive, a made-up invoicing app. Overnight the diff finds two changes on its pricing page: "Pro plan: $29/month" became "Pro plan: $35/month", and "Recieve invoices" became "Receive invoices".

Your agent sends just those lines with one rule: in 2 sentences, say what changed and quote the line. Back comes: "Tidyhive raised its Pro plan from $29 to $35 a month, about 21% more (source: 'Pro plan: $35/month'). The other change fixes a spelling mistake and doesn't matter."

**Two edits that look the same, very different news**: one costs each customer $72 a year, and the other fixes the word *receive*.
cards.simpler: Overnight, two lines changed on the pricing page of Tidyhive, a made-up invoicing app. "Pro plan: $29/month" became "$35/month", and "Recieve" became "Receive". The agent sends just those lines and asks for 2 sentences that quote the line. The reply says Pro went from $29 to $35 a month, about 21% more, and quotes the new line. It says the other edit only fixes a spelling mistake. **Two edits that look the same, very different news**: one costs each customer $72 a year.

cards.prompt: You're writing the instruction your agent sends with each diff. Which one does the job?

options.text: "Here's the changed text. Tell me everything interesting about this company."
"Here are the added and removed lines. In 2 sentences, say what changed. Quote the line each claim comes from."
"Here are both full pages. Summarise the differences."

whyNot.a: That's an open question, not a strict rule. 'Everything interesting' invites the model to guess beyond the clipping.
whyNot.c: That's both whole newspapers again, not the clipping. The diff already found the differences, so the model would be redoing that job, and less reliably.

cards.reteach: A good prompt here has two parts: only the changed lines, and a strict rule. The rule gives a number (2 sentences) and asks for a quote, so the answer comes back short and easy to check.

cards.title: Strict beats polite
cards.body:
The second half of the prompt is the rule, and strict works better than polite. Say "2 sentences", not "a short summary". A number is something the model can count. Without a limit, a one-line price change can come back as three paragraphs about *market positioning*.

The other rule matters most: **quote the source line**. The quote is the tag stapled to each clipping saying which paper and which page it came from. You can check the claim in five seconds, and the model has to stick to what's in front of it.

No quote? Treat the claim as a rumour.
cards.simpler: For the rule, strict works better than polite. Say "2 sentences", not "a short summary", because a number is something the model can count. Without one, a one-line price change can turn into three paragraphs. The most important rule: **quote the source line**. It's like the tag on a clipping that shows its paper and page. You can check it in five seconds, and the model has to stick to what's in front of it. No quote? Treat the claim as a rumour.

cards.body: Sam figured more context couldn't hurt, so Sam's agent pasted both full pricing pages into the prompt. The note came back cheerful and sure of itself: Tidyhive had "launched a free trial". That free trial had been on the page since March. **Spot it by checking the quote**: if the quoted line isn't in the diff, the model was reading the old newspaper, not the clipping.
cards.simpler: Sam thought more context couldn't hurt, so Sam's agent pasted both full pricing pages into the prompt. The note came back cheerful and sure of itself: Tidyhive had "launched a free trial". But that free trial had been on the page since March. **Spot it by checking the quote**. If the quoted line isn't in the diff, the model read the old newspaper instead of the clipping.

cards.prompt: A friend sees your agent's daily notes and asks how they stay so short and so trustworthy. Which answer is the real reason?

options.text: "I give it the whole site, so it never misses anything."
"It only sees the changed lines, and it has to quote the line behind each claim."
"I let it write as much as it likes, then trim the answer myself."

whyNot.a: That's the whole newspaper, not the clipping. More text gives the model more to guess about, not less.
whyNot.c: That's trimming afterwards, not a rule up front. The 2-sentence limit belongs in the prompt, so the model does the cutting.

cards.reteach: The notes stay short because the 2-sentence rule is written into the prompt. They stay trustworthy because the model only sees what changed, and every claim has to point at a real line.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Don't hand the model the whole page. Hand it **only the lines that changed, plus a strict rule**: 2 sentences, and quote the line you're relying on. Less text means less guessing, and the quote lets you check every claim in seconds.

Tomorrow: the alarm clock goes on, and the agent runs without you.
cards.simpler: Don't give the model the whole page. Give it **only the lines that changed, plus a strict rule**: 2 sentences, and quote the line you're relying on. Less text means less guessing. The quote lets you check every claim in seconds, like a tag that shows where a clipping came from. Tomorrow the alarm clock goes on, and the agent runs without you.

cards.body: Open any AI chat you already use. Paste an old line and a new line, like "$29/month" and "$35/month". Ask: "In 2 sentences, say what changed. Quote the line you used." Check whether it quotes.
cards.simpler: Open any AI chat you already use. Paste an old line and a new line, such as "$29/month" and "$35/month". Then ask: "In 2 sentences, say what changed. Quote the line you used." Read the answer and **check whether it quotes**. If it does, you can see exactly which line its answer came from.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now write a prompt that turns a diff into a 2-sentence plain-English summary with a quoted source line.
